extra.message: Hardcoded default APP_SECRET_KEY enables session and API key forgery if not overridden in production — Complete authentication bypass — forge session tokens for any user, forge API keys for any vendor. [verified: Config.py line 13 defaults APP_SECRET_KEY to 'local-dev-secret-change-me' when the env var is absent; this key is used by hash_token() in security.py for HMAC-SHA256 on all session/CSRF/API-key/reset-token/webhook-secret hashes, and no startup check or runtime guard prevents production use of the default.]

Hardcoded Default Secret Key Allows Token Forgery — Attackers can forge session tokens to impersonate any user (including marketplace_admin), forge API keys, and forge password reset tokens. [verified: Config.py line 13 defaults APP_SECRET_KEY to 'local-dev-secret-change-me' when the env var is absent; this key is used by hash_token() in security.py for HMAC-SHA256 on all session/CSRF/API-key/reset-token/webhook-secret hashes, and no startup check or runtime guard prevents production use of the default.]

Default Hardcoded Application Secret Key — Session token forgery enabling impersonation of any user including administrator accounts. [verified: Config.py line 13 defaults APP_SECRET_KEY to 'local-dev-secret-change-me' when the env var is absent; this key is used by hash_token() in security.py for HMAC-SHA256 on all session/CSRF/API-key/reset-token/webhook-secret hashes, and no startup check or runtime guard prevents production use of the default.]

Password reset token leaked in API response enabling full account takeover — Complete account takeover of any user by requesting password reset and using the token returned in the response. [verified: password_reset_request (line 710) generates a real cryptographically-random token with new_token('reset_'), stores its hash in the DB, and returns the raw token as mock_reset_token in the unauthenticated response body — any caller can request a reset for any email and immediately use the returned token on /api/auth/password-reset/confirm to set a new password, achieving full account takeover.]

Server-Side Template Injection (SSTI) in ops Jinja2 endpoint — Remote code execution, arbitrary file read, and full server compromise via Jinja2 SSTI. [verified: Same SSTI as finding 1: `fragment` is concatenated into Jinja2 template source at line 102 and rendered, allowing server-side code execution via injected template expressions.]

Server-side template injection (SSTI) via user-controlled Jinja2 template fragment — Remote code execution on the application server via Jinja2 SSTI gadgets. [verified: Query parameter `fragment` is concatenated into a Jinja2 Template source string at line 102 (`Template('Result: ' + fragment).render()`) rather than passed as a variable, allowing SSTI payloads like `{{config.__class__.__init__.__globals__}}` to achieve RCE.]

OS Command Injection via ping host parameter — Remote code execution on the application server, leading to full system compromise, data exfiltration, or lateral movement. [verified: Same command injection as findings 0/9: unsanitized `host` query parameter concatenated into `os.system('ping -c 1 ' + host)` at line 140, gated only by x-internal-token.]

Missing Rate Limiting on Authentication Endpoints — Attackers can perform unlimited brute-force password guessing, credential stuffing, and account enumeration without throttling. [verified: Identical to finding [1]: no rate limiting on any auth endpoint — no middleware, no decorator, no counter found anywhere in main.py, deps.py, or config.py.]

Missing rate limiting on login, registration, and password-reset endpoints enabling brute-force attacks — Brute-force password guessing on login; brute-force password-reset token guessing; mass account registration abuse. [verified: No rate-limiting mechanism exists anywhere in the codebase — no middleware in main.py, no decorators in deps.py, no in-memory/Redis counters, and grep for 'rate.limit|throttl|slowapi|brute.force' returns zero results — leaving /api/auth/login, /register, /password-reset/request, and /password-reset/confirm fully open to unlimited brute-force attacks.]

Path Traversal Arbitrary File Write via packet_ref parameter — Arbitrary file write on the filesystem leading to code execution, configuration tampering, or denial of service. [verified: Same path traversal as findings 5/13: `packet_ref` at line 28 used directly in filesystem path with no sanitization, allowing request body to be written to arbitrary locations via `../` traversal.]

Missing Authentication on Internal Ops Endpoint — An unauthenticated attacker can access an internal operations endpoint that exposes an internal operations memo and reflects attacker-controlled input, bypassing the INTERNAL_OPS_TOKEN gate protecting all other /ops routes. [verified: The `/ops/fold/seller-payout-fold-084` route at line 39 is the only ops endpoint missing `Depends(_wrk_gate)` — all other 17 endpoints require the x-internal-token check, making this endpoint reachable without any authentication.]

Path Traversal Arbitrary File Write via name parameter — Arbitrary file write on the filesystem, potentially enabling code execution or data corruption. [verified: Same path traversal as findings 6/12: `name` parameter at line 115 used unsanitized in `BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name` with `target.parent.mkdir(parents=True)`, enabling arbitrary file writes.]

NoSQL Injection via unsanitized MongoDB find_one query — Bypass of query logic, unauthorized data access, potential remote code execution via $where operator. [verified: Same NoSQL injection as findings 4/15: unsanitized user JSON passed as MongoDB `find_one` query at line 136, allowing $where/$regex/$ne operator injection.]

Path Traversal in seller_dock_shelf_597 allows arbitrary file write — An attacker with the internal ops token can write arbitrary files to any location on the filesystem, potentially achieving remote code execution via cron jobs, SSH authorized_keys, or overwriting application source code. [verified: Query parameter `name` is used directly in path construction at line 115: `target = BASE_EXPORT_DIR / name` with no path traversal prevention, and `target.parent.mkdir(parents=True)` creates directories along traversal paths, enabling arbitrary file writes.]

XML External Entity (XXE) Injection via lxml parser with entity resolution enabled — Arbitrary local file read, internal network SSRF, denial of service, and potential information disclosure. [verified: Same XXE as findings 2/11: lxml parser at line 131 configured with entity resolution and DTD loading enabled on attacker-supplied XML, enabling file reads and SSRF.]

NoSQL Injection via user-controlled MongoDB query in seller_mongo_lane_610 — An attacker with the internal ops token can execute arbitrary MongoDB queries including JavaScript evaluation, bypass access controls, exfiltrate data, or cause denial of service via resource-intensive queries. [verified: User-controlled JSON body is passed directly as a MongoDB query at line 136: `query = payload.get('filter', payload); ...find_one(query)` with no operator allowlist, enabling $where, $regex, or $ne injection to bypass query logic or exfiltrate data.]

Missing Security Headers — HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options, and X-Content-Type-Options — Application is vulnerable to clickjacking (no frame-ancestors/X-Frame-Options), MIME sniffing attacks (no X-Content-Type-Options), and lacks protection against script injection via CSP and HTTPS enforcement via HSTS. [verified: The FastAPI app configures only CORS middleware (lines 66–72) and sets no HSTS, CSP, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, Referrer-Policy, or Permissions-Policy headers anywhere, leaving all responses without these protections on every reachable HTTP path.]

Missing Secure Flag on Session Cookies by Default — Session cookies can be transmitted over plaintext HTTP, enabling session hijacking via network sniffing or man-in-the-middle attacks. [verified: set_auth_cookies (line 278) sets secure=settings.cookie_secure which defaults to False (COOKIE_SECURE env var defaults to 'false' in config.py line 16) — session_token cookies are transmitted without the Secure flag by default, allowing interception over plaintext HTTP.]

User Enumeration via Registration Endpoint — Attackers can enumerate valid user email addresses to build target lists for phishing, credential stuffing, or password spraying. [verified: Identical to finding [2]: POST /api/auth/register returns distinct 409 'Email already registered' vs 201, enabling unauthenticated email enumeration.]

Account Enumeration via Registration Error Message — Enumeration of valid user accounts facilitating targeted attacks. [verified: Identical to findings [2] and [8]: registration endpoint returns 409 with 'Email already registered' on duplicate email, enabling unauthenticated account enumeration.]

User account enumeration via registration endpoint error differentiation — An attacker can compile a list of valid user emails on the platform for targeted phishing or credential-stuffing attacks. [verified: The register endpoint (line 686) returns HTTP 409 'Email already registered' when the email exists vs 201 on success, with no normalization or generic error — an unauthenticated caller can probe emails and distinguish registered from unregistered accounts.]

Missing session invalidation on password reset allows stolen sessions to persist — An attacker who possesses a stolen session token before a password reset can continue to use it after the reset, maintaining unauthorized access to the victim's account indefinitely (until the session naturally expires). [verified: Same code as finding [3]: password_reset_confirm (line 714) only updates password_hash and clears reset_token fields — no SessionToken.revoked_at is set, so existing stolen sessions survive the password reset.]

Sensitive Payout Data Exposure via Public Vendor Listing — An attacker can enumerate vendors in non-public statuses (suspended, rejected, pending_verification) and retrieve their masked bank account details, payout holder names, and tax ID last-4 digits — financial data that should not be publicly accessible. [verified: Identical to finding [5]: the public GET /api/vendors endpoint (line 884) accepts an unauthenticated status filter of type VendorStatus and returns serialize_vendor output including payout_destination_masked, payout_holder_name, and tax_id_last4 for vendors in any status including suspended/rejected.]

Sensitive payout metadata exposed to unauthenticated users via public vendor endpoints — Anonymous users can enumerate all active vendors and collect their masked bank account destination details, payout holder names, and tax ID last-4 digits. While masked, this financial metadata should not be publicly accessible and aids in social engineering or credential-stuffing attacks against vendors. [verified: serialize_vendor (line 337-339) unconditionally includes payout_destination_masked, payout_holder_name, and tax_id_last4, and both list_public_vendors (line 884) and vendor_storefront (line 1008) use this serializer with no auth guard — additionally the status query param on list_public_vendors accepts any VendorStatus, allowing enumeration of suspended/rejected vendors' financial metadata.]

CSV formula injection in administrative data exports — Code execution in spreadsheet applications (Excel, LibreOffice, Google Sheets) when administrators open exported CSV files containing attacker-crafted values. [verified: csv_response (line 1846) uses csv.DictWriter.writerows() without prefix-char escaping; vendor-imported CSV product titles (line 1183, no sanitization) flow into admin inventory exports (line 1852) — when an admin opens the CSV in a spreadsheet, cells starting with =,+,-,@ execute as formulas.]

CSV Formula Injection in Admin Export Endpoints — Remote code execution on the machine of an administrator who opens the exported CSV in a spreadsheet application, potentially leading to credential theft or malware execution. [verified: Identical to finding [4]: csv_response (line 1846) writes rows via csv.DictWriter without formula-character escaping, and user-controlled fields like product titles (settable via CSV import at line 1183) appear in admin exports at /api/admin/exports/{kind}.csv.]

CSV Formula Injection in Vendor Inventory Export — Code execution in spreadsheet applications when an administrator or vendor opens the exported inventory CSV, enabling data exfiltration or malware delivery. [verified: csv_response() writes vendor-controlled product.title via csv.DictWriter with zero sanitization of formula-leading characters (=, +, -, @); the same unsanitized CSV path is also used by admin_export_csv (inventory kind, line ~1938) where a malicious vendor title reaches an admin opener, and no sanitization utility exists in security.py.]

Open Redirect via unsanitized lane parameter — Phishing attacks, credential theft, and bypass of URL allowlist restrictions. [verified: Same open redirect as findings 7/17: `lane` query parameter passed unsanitized to `RedirectResponse(lane)` at line 45, enabling phishing via external-domain redirects.]

Mass Assignment via unfiltered workset.update(payload) — Unauthorized modification of application state fields, potential privilege escalation. [verified: Same mass assignment as finding 8: `workset.update(payload)` at line 54 merges entire JSON body with no field allowlist, allowing override of role/approved/balance fields.]

Log Injection and Bearer Token Exposure via Request Logging — Log forgery to mislead audit trails, and exposure of bearer authentication tokens in application logs. [verified: Line 57 logs raw request body and Authorization header at WARNING level with no sanitization, enabling both log injection (newlines in body forge log entries) and credential exposure (bearer tokens in plaintext).]

Sensitive Bearer Token Logged in Application Logs — Exposure of API key or session bearer tokens in application logs, enabling credential theft and unauthorized access. [verified: Same sensitive data logging as finding 3: Authorization header value logged in plaintext at WARNING level at line 57, exposing bearer tokens to log consumers.]

Bearer token and request body logged in plaintext to application logs — Exposure of API keys or other credentials in log files readable by anyone with log access. [verified: Line 57 logs the full Authorization header value at WARNING level: `logger.warning('ops tally body=%s bearer=%s', body, request.headers.get('authorization'))` — bearer tokens are written to application logs in plaintext.]

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) via Jinja2 |safe filter with user-controlled input — Execution of arbitrary JavaScript in the browser of anyone viewing the response, cookie theft, session hijacking, or phishing. SSTI chaining may also enable server-side code execution. [verified: Same XSS as finding 14: `card` parameter rendered with Jinja2 `|safe` filter at line 81, disabling HTML escaping and enabling script injection in the browser.]

Permissive CORS with Credentialed Access in ops mirror endpoint — Cross-origin attacks — any website can make authenticated requests to this endpoint with the victim's credentials, enabling data theft or state-changing operations. [verified: Endpoint at line 94 sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` to the request's Origin header and `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`; for simple GET requests the main app's CORSMiddleware does not strip these permissive headers, allowing credentialed cross-origin reads from any origin.]

CORS Misconfiguration — Reflected Origin with Credentials — Cross-origin data theft when a victim visits a malicious site, enabling attackers to read sensitive responses from the ops endpoint. [verified: Same CORS misconfiguration as finding 18: reflected Origin header with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true` at line 94 bypasses main app's CORSMiddleware for simple GET requests.]

Weak Random Number Generator (random.choice) for Token Generation — Predictable token values enabling token forgery if the generated values are used in security contexts. [verified: Same weak PRNG as finding 19: `random.choice()` at line 118 generates predictable codes; Mersenne Twister is not cryptographically secure for token generation.]
